title: Gandhi: An Autobiography – The Story of My Experiments with Truth
author: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi
edition_analyzed: Most widely used English translation by Mahadev Desai
target_audience: Readers interested in world history and Indian independence
Students of philosophy and nonviolent resistance
Followers of political and religious leaders
Individuals seeking personal inspiration or spiritual guidance
primary_purpose: To narrate Gandhi's personal journey, revealing his moral, spiritual, and philosophical development, as well as the principles and 'experiments' that guided his public life and the Indian independence movement.

structure_format.narrative_style: First-person, reflective, candid, often humble and self-critical
structure_format.organization: Chronological, divided into five parts (Foreword and Parts I–V), with brief chapters focused on key episodes, people, and lessons
features: Explanations of moral and religious beliefs
Anecdotes illustrating ethical dilemmas and experiments
Descriptive passages about family, comrades, and sociopolitical context

key_concepts_lessons: A continual process of self-examination and self-correction shapes character.
Truth and nonviolence are not simply ideals, but practical guiding principles.
Spirituality is deeply intertwined with public action and reform.
Political activism is rooted in personal integrity and community service.
Experimentation and humility are essential for growth.
Simple living, vegetarianism, and celibacy are central to personal discipline.
notable_features: Focus on candid, personal anecdotes and philosophical inquiry
Unique blending of autobiography and treatise on ethics
Explicit discussion of personal failures and doubts
Foundation for later global nonviolent movements
cultural_historical_context: Written during the late 1920s as India’s struggle for independence from British colonial rule intensified. Gandhi's philosophy of nonviolence influenced major civil rights movements worldwide, notably those led by Martin Luther King Jr. and Nelson Mandela.
reception_impact: Regarded as one of the most important autobiographies of the 20th century
Inspirational text for political leaders, activists, and ordinary readers
Key source for understanding Gandhi’s character, strategies, and mindset
Influenced discourse on nonviolence, ethics, and political liberation
Praised for its humility, honesty, and moral vision
comparable_titles: Long Walk to Freedom by Nelson Mandela
The Diary of a Young Girl by Anne Frank
The Story of My Life by Helen Keller
Autobiography of Martin Luther King, Jr. by Clayborne Carson (ed.)
